subject: Three Funerals and a Death
body: View this post on the web at [URL] Sunday, August 16th, 2026 Laramie, Wyoming By Dan Denning â€˜No, I didnâ€™t say I would have punched Richard Nixon in the face.â€™ â€˜I said if Iâ€™d known then what I know now, I might have said something at the time.â€™ â€˜Said what, though?â€™ Iâ€™ll come back to this conversation shortly. But it will only make sense to you if you understand what happened 55 years ago this weekend. Historians call it â€˜The Nixon Shock.â€™ But it was more like the first of three funerals and a death. The worst part is, what began happening to the value of your savings then from the White Houseâ€¦may be happening again. Are you ready for it? Sunday, August 15th, 1971. Itâ€™s 9pm Eastern Standard time. Live from the Oval Office, President Richard Nixon pre-empts NBCâ€™s Bonanza with a televised address to the nation. He announces three measures to take effect immediately. First, a 10% â€˜surchargeâ€™ on imports to the US. There were some exceptions. But the official inflation figure in the US was 5.84% a year (itâ€™s 3.4% today according to the July numbers from the BLS). Second, a 90-day â€˜freezeâ€™ on wages and prices. This was a â€˜time outâ€™ meant to halt inflation in its tracks. The â€˜shockâ€™ was the third thing. Nixon immediately suspended the convertibility of US dollars into gold. It was targeted toward the British andthe French. Both countries had been redeeming dollars for gold at a faster rate. Theyâ€™d watched the growth of US debt and deficits from the war in Vietnam and an expanding federal government. The â€˜shockâ€™ was meant to be temporary (a shock that continues is more like an electrocution). But as history sees it now, it was the first of three â€˜deathsâ€™ for the US dollar. The second death came with the Smithsonian Agreement in December of the same year. It re-set the statutory price of gold from $35 to $38. It was intended to stabilize the value of the dollar. It lasted fourteen months. In February 1973 the dollar was devalued again, from $38/oz to $42.22/oz. Thatâ€™s where it sits today. And if you think it sounds weird the President or the Secretary of the Treasury can arbitrarily â€˜setâ€™ the price of an ounce of gold, it IS weird. These days it is largely for accounting purposes, to establish a value for the gold owned by the Treasury and stored (we hope) at places like Fort Knox and West Point. By 1976, it was official. The US dollar was no longer backed, in any sense, by gold. No one could redeem US paper for real metal. The world had moved beyond the post-World War II Bretton Woods system to a system of free floating exchange rates, where currency values were determined by a combination of interest rates, GDP growth, and government deficits. Government deficits (and the national debt) are obviously a MUCH bigger problem today (the government debt-to-GDP ratio was 35% at the end of 1971â€¦itâ€™s 125% today). That makes another devaluation more likely. Perhaps soon. Remember, every devaluation

Editorial: Last Week in AI: The Cursor Acquisition, New Grok and GLM Models, Anthropicâ€™s Latest Deal, and River AI There was a time when following AI was relatively simple. A new model appeared, someone posted a benchmark table, and we updated the leaderboard in our heads. That mental model is rapidly becoming obsolete. Consider what happened this week. SpaceX officially closed its $60 billion acquisition of Cursor, one of the defining products of the AI coding era. At almost the same time, SpaceXAI released Grok 4.6, a model explicitly optimized for long-running agents, coding, and multi-step knowledge work. The important detail is not that Grok moved a few points on a benchmark. It is that Grok now flows directly into Cursor, Grok Build, GitHub Copilot, APIs, and autonomous agents. The model is becoming the stack. Think of the early cloud era. AWS did not win because EC2 had the prettiest virtual machine. It won because compute became attached to storage, databases, networking, identity and eventually an enormous developer ecosystem. Intelligence appears to be following the same path. Anthropic seems to understand this. The company is reportedly discussing a roughly $6 billion acquisition of Decart AI, which works on model infrastructure, world models and compute optimization. The deal is not finalized, but the direction is interesting: one of the strongest model companies is reaching down the stack toward the machinery required to produce intelligence more efficiently. Meanwhile, the frontier itself keeps getting more crowded. Chinaâ€™s Z.ai announced GLM-5.3, showing surprisingly strong cybersecurity capabilities and again demonstrating how quickly open-weight models are compressing the gap with closed systems. If the first phase of the AI race was about discovering how to build frontier models, the second may be about how quickly everyone else can reproduce the recipe. And then there is River AI, founded by former xAI co-founder Igor Babuschkin, which raised an extraordinary $1.1 billion this week. Riverâ€™s thesis is almost the mirror image of the giant labs: instead of renting intelligence from one enormous generic model, companies and individuals should train models on their own data, rewards and preferencesâ€”and ultimately own the resulting intelligence. subject: The weird roots of wokeness
sender: Nick Cohen from Writing from London <nickcohen@substack.com>
body: View this post on the web at [URL] Jason Arday in 2024 before his world fell apart [CREDIT WIKI COMMONS [ [URL] ]] This piece is for paying subscribers, and so I need to say that, if you sign up for an annual subscription, you receive access to all articles, archives, and debates at a cost of Â£1.40 ($1.15) a week. While I am away on my travels, I am updating pieces that have a contemporary relevance. Today I look at the origins of wokeness. The awful death of Jason Arday shows that they could not be more relevant. Cambridge University threw out all considerations of appointment based on merit when it made him its Professor of Sociology. He met its diversity criteria, and they mattered more. The media exposed his plagiarism and lies. Good â€“ thatâ€™s its job. But the press and online right then mounted a cancel campaign of insane intensity. The Times alone published 44 stories on Arday, far more than it runs on actual war criminals. When I was on the receiving end of cancel culture, I felt that at a subconscious level the pack yearned for its targetâ€™s death. Jason Arday duly killed himself. Meanwhile, in the United States Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez prepared to run for president by jettisoning the baggage of the woke movement [ [URL] ]she knew made her unpopular. But what was she jettisoning? And what motivates progressive bosses at institutions like Cambridge? Below I make what, I hope, is a reasoned explanation about why the ideology that came out of American academia represented such a break with older left-wing ideas. The socialist tradition was materialist, for example. Under the influence of postmodernism, the new left holds that the material reality of biological sex is an oppressive construct, which we are free to reject if we wish. The traditional liberal-left believed in abolishing racism by treating people equally without regard for colour or creed. Critical race theory condemns this colour-blindness as a swindle that hides white supremacy. It results in special schemes to give priority to members of minorities, which provoke a right-wing backlash because they conflict with basic notions of fairness â€“ this, in essence, is poor Jason Ardayâ€™s story. But I am running ahead of myself. Let us begin at the beginning. Identitarian Politics: A Guide for the Confused There are two dishonest conversations about wokeness, or identity politics if you prefer the less contentious term. The first from conservatives is wearily familiar. For some on the right â€œwokeâ€ is now a synonym for â€œanything I canâ€™t abideâ€. Overuse has made the insult meaningless. On the left, the dishonesty lies in the denial that a new ideology even exists. Nothing has chang

body: View this post on the web at [URL] Good morning from London. We are looking for an outstanding economist to join us as an AI Economy Research Fellow [ [URL] ]. If you know someone we should speak to, send them our way. Cheers The AI spend of your nightmares Amazon spent some $1.8 million [ [URL] ] on a Claude project that ran for five months. A senior employee said [ [URL] ]: â€œItâ€™s difficult to figure out how much anything [AI-related] costsâ€. We had a similar experience with R Mini Arnold, my OpenClaw agent. Its costs have run up as it has grown in complexity, and it takes time to switch it to progressively cheaper models. It becomes hard to keep track of exactly what is running efficiently and what isnâ€™t. Nathan Warren called out an outrageous few days when the bot blew through $500 a day. The subsequent tedious audit was worth it. Many processes were running older, higher-tier models, like Opus 4.5, which are more expensive than smaller, newer models like Sonnet 5 or a slew of open-weight models. The price war that has broken out between Anthropic and OpenAI in response to Chinese advances has helped [ [URL] ] even more. By default, RMA now uses my token allowance on OpenAI Codex, which is already paid for in my $200-a-month subscription. It will fall back to DeepSeek v4 Flash or Pro if OpenAI is unavailable. For harder tasks, it can jump to 5.6 Sol, OpenAIâ€™s top model, through the same subscription or Kimi K3 or Anthropicâ€™s Fable (both of which I pay for by the token). The net result is $6 a day, lower than it has been for months. The funny thing is that RMA is cheaper than it ever has been and yet more capable than ever. It plugs into the Manus API for some types of work; Claude Code and Codex for coding tasks; Prism (our internal research graph, which is more powerful than ever); and other resources like Elicit for academic papers. Itâ€™s a microcosm of the big question in the industry. Has $494 a day just disappeared from genAI revenue? In some sense, yes, but that was really an anomaly. RMA had typically cost me $50 to $60 a day before it went wild. Even at $6 a day, it runs to $2k per year from me alone, which is reasonably substantial for someone who isnâ€™t writing code. I expect spending to spike as I move back into book-writing terrain and need more research done. Iâ€™m curious whether readers have had similar experiences. See also: The cost of tokenmaxxing [ [URL]
summary: The author discusses the cost of using AI models, specifically the costs associated with their OpenClaw agent R Mini Arnold, and how they have managed to reduce costs.

body: ---------- -------------------- For several years, we have kept returning to the same paper at Turing Post. It was published in April 2023 under the title _Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior_, although most people remember it simply as Smallville. The researchers placed 25 AI characters inside a pixelated town, gave them occupations, relationships, memories, and daily routines, then observed what happened. We have cited it in our articles on [agent memory]([URL] [profiling]([URL] [multi-agent systems]([URL] and [agent social networks]([URL] A simulated town called Smallville has practically been living in our archive. It gave a concrete form to an idea that was still hard to picture in 2023: an LLM could become more than a chatbot when it was given a persistent history and placed inside an environment with other agents. View image: ([URL] [generative agents] Caption: Remember this image? Image credit: [This phenomenol paper]([URL] Now this town has grown into **Simile AI **â€“ **a company with a $2 billion valuation in less than six months.** And the company wants to simulate all eight billion people on Earth. Simile CEO describes the long-term ambition as a "CERN of human society" â€“ bank runs, climate cooperation, democratic collapse â€“ and imagines a single foundational simulation that might one day cost $100 million and take months to run.
